case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a noncitizen who did not receive an initial Notice to Appear containing the hearing’s time and place can nevertheless be ordered removed in absentia (or be denied rescission) when the government later sent a notice of hearing with the correct time and place and the noncitizen failed to appear.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act provisions governing notice and in absentia removal/rescission: 8 U.S.C. § 1229(a)(1) (Notice to Appear requirements), § 1229(a)(2) (later notice of hearing/time-place changes), and § 1229a(b)(5) (in absentia removal and rescission for lack of notice).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Campos-Chaves (and similarly Singh/Mendez-Colín in the consolidated matters) argue that the statutory scheme requires a single, compliant Notice to Appear under § 1229(a)(1) that includes the time and place of the hearing, and that if the government instead used a two-step notice process (a deficient NTA followed by a later hearing notice), an in absentia removal order cannot stand (or must be rescinded) because the noncitizen did not receive the “notice in accordance with paragraph (1)” contemplated by § 1229a(b)(5), making the removal order unlawful even if a later notice of hearing provided the missing time-and-place information.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that in absentia removal turns on whether the person had actual notice of the hearing they missed; if the government provided the hearing’s time and place through a later notice under § 1229(a)(2) and the noncitizen then failed to attend, the noncitizen cannot obtain rescission by pointing to defects in the earlier NTA, because § 1229a(b)(5) permits in absentia removal when notice was provided under paragraph (1) or paragraph (2), and the statute’s text, context, and practical administration support treating a later time-and-place notice as sufficient notice for in absentia purposes (with deference to the agency’s reasonable interpretation if any ambiguity remains).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “no change, no paragraph (2)” point is the hardest: § 1229(a)(2) is styled as a change-or-postponement notice, and it is awkward to treat it as a free-standing substitute for an initially defective § 1229(a)(1) NTA. But § 1229a(b)(5) asks a hearing-specific question—whether the Government provided written notice for the missed hearing “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)”—and, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress, importing Pereira/Niz-Chavez’s single-document rule from the stop-time context would effectively nullify Congress’s express “or (2)” in this distinct in absentia/rescission scheme. A minimalist, institutionally cautious path is to hold only that when the Government proves proper service of a later writing that supplies the actual time and place (and statutory warnings) for the hearing that was missed, rescission under § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) is unavailable notwithstanding an earlier § 1229(a)(1) defect—without opining more broadly on jurisdiction or on cases lacking proof of receipt. On that narrow ground, Sotomayor’s sequencing concern does not overcome the disjunctive text Congress chose for in absentia orders.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presses a serious textual point that § 1229(a)(2) contemplates a “change or postponement,” and thus seems ill-suited to supply initial time-and-place information when the original NTA omitted it. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(A) and (C)(ii) do not ask whether the proceeding was initiated by a pristine § 1229(a)(1) document; they ask whether the noncitizen received “written notice … in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)” for the hearing that was missed, and we are not at liberty to read the “or (2)” out of the statute. Pereira and Niz-Chavez construed the stop-time rule’s distinct trigger—service of “a notice to appear under § 1229(a)(1)”—and do not justify importing a single-document requirement into § 1229a(b)(5)’s expressly disjunctive notice scheme. On an original public meaning reading of the in absentia and rescission provisions, actual receipt of a later written notice supplying the operative time and place defeats rescission under § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best textual point is that § 1229(a)(2) is styled as a notice of “change or postponement,” and she argues that where the initial NTA lacked any time/place there was nothing to “change.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(A) and (C)(ii) ask a hearing-specific question and use Congress’s disjunctive formulation—notice “under paragraph (1) or (2)”—which is difficult to square with a categorical rule that an initial paragraph (1) defect voids an in absentia order even when the respondent actually received a later written notice specifying the time and place of the missed hearing. Pereira and Niz-Chavez interpreted the stop-time rule’s distinct trigger (“a notice to appear under § 1229(a)(1)”) and do not justify importing a single-document requirement into § 1229a(b)(5) in a way that effectively nullifies Congress’s explicit “or (2)” language. On a textualist reading attentive to statutory structure and practical consequences, properly served operative hearing notice suffices for in absentia removal and defeats rescission notwithstanding an earlier defective NTA.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point that § 1229a(b)(5) is hearing-focused and uses a disjunctive—notice “under paragraph (1) or (2)”—which seems to allow reliance on a later notice for the missed hearing. But that reading only works by stripping § 1229(a)(2) of its defining feature: it is notice of a “change or postponement,” and where the Government never set a time/place in the first instance, there is nothing to change, so treating (2) as a free-standing initial notice rewrites the statute’s sequence and dilutes Congress’s notice safeguards. Pereira and especially Niz-Chavez reinforce that when Congress prescribes a particular form of notice with time-and-place specificity, courts should not convert agency convenience into a cure that predictably increases confusion and in absentia removals among people least able to navigate shifting paperwork. The respondent’s approach may be administratively workable, but under a fair-process, real-world-impacts lens it invites exactly the kind of notice failures Congress sought to prevent, so I would hold rescission available when the initiating notice was never compliant and (2) cannot lawfully do the curing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that § 1229(a)(2) is worded as notice of a “change,” so treating it as a free-standing substitute for an initially compliant § 1229(a)(1) NTA creates textual friction. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5) is hearing-specific and expressly authorizes in absentia removal (and limits rescission) when written notice was provided “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2),” and importing Pereira/Niz-Chavez’s single-document rule would effectively erase the “or (2)” option Congress wrote. Even accepting the “change” awkwardness, the more coherent statutory reading—consistent with the in absentia scheme’s focus on actual notice of the missed hearing—is that a properly served later notice supplying the operative time/place qualifies as notice “in accordance with” paragraph (2) for § 1229a(b)(5) purposes. On my pragmatic textualist approach, that construction best harmonizes the provisions and avoids turning an initiating defect into a categorical rescission entitlement despite actual hearing notice.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presses a serious textual point that § 1229(a)(2) is styled as notice of a “change,” so it is awkward to treat it as a universal cure when the Government’s initial § 1229(a)(1) notice never supplied a time or place. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(A) and (C)(ii) pose a narrower, hearing-specific inquiry: whether the Government proved the noncitizen received the written notice required “under paragraph (1) or (2)” for the proceeding at which the in absentia order entered, and the disjunctive “or” is text we must respect. Pereira and Niz-Chavez interpreted a different trigger—service of “a notice to appear under § 1229(a)(1)”—and I do not see a principled textual basis to transpose their single-document rule into § 1229a(b)(5)’s differently worded scheme. The “change” phrasing in (a)(2) creates some tension, but it is insufficient to justify rewriting Congress’s express “(1) or (2)” formulation into an implicit “(1) and (2).”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that § 1229(a)(2) is styled as notice of a “change,” and it sits awkwardly when the initial NTA never listed a time or place. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 1229a(b)(5) is a distinct, hearing-focused scheme that authorizes in absentia orders (and limits rescission) when the Government proves the noncitizen received written notice “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2),” and that express disjunction is hard to square with a categorical rule that an initial NTA defect voids an in absentia order despite actual later time-and-place notice. I agree with Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan that Pereira and Niz-Chavez are best confined to the stop-time/cancellation context keyed to “a notice to appear under § 1229(a)(1),” and we should not extend a single-document requirement to a different statutory provision that expressly contemplates paragraph (2) notice. Institutionally and as a matter of workability, tying rescission to whether the respondent actually received operative notice of the missed hearing better fits Congress’s design and avoids turning technical initiation defects into automatic rescission even when meaningful notice was provided.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “no change, no paragraph (2)” point is the best textual objection, because § 1229(a)(2) presupposes an earlier time/place from which a “change or postponement” can occur. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(A) and (C)(ii) set a hearing-specific predicate—whether the Government gave written notice for the hearing that was missed “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)”—and that disjunctive text is difficult to square with an atextual, categorical single-document prerequisite for in absentia orders. Pereira and Niz-Chavez, as Justice Gorsuch notes, construed the stop-time rule’s different trigger (“a notice to appear under § 1229(a)(1)”) and do not compel importing a one-document rule into § 1229a(b)(5) where Congress expressly referenced paragraph (2). On an originalist/textualist reading, the better fit is that a properly served later writing providing the operative time/place can satisfy the notice condition for the missed hearing even if the initial NTA was defective for other purposes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point about § 1229(a)(2)’s “change or postponement” trigger is the hardest statutory obstacle, because it suggests paragraph (2) presupposes a valid initial time-and-place setting. But I am persuaded by Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice that § 1229a(b)(5)’s in absentia/rescission scheme is expressly hearing-focused and disjunctive—turning on whether written notice for the missed hearing was provided “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)”—so importing Pereira/Niz-Chavez’s single-document rule from the stop-time context would effectively nullify Congress’s “or (2)” language here. On a procedural-fairness and pragmatic view, where the Government proves proper service of a later writing that actually specified the hearing’s time/place and consequences, rescission would remedy a technical defect without a proportional due-process gain. I would therefore affirm on a narrow ground tied to receipt of operative notice for the hearing that resulted in the in absentia order, without endorsing broader agency shortcuts in other contexts.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(A) authorizes in absentia removal when written notice was provided “under paragraph (1) or (2)” of § 1229(a), and § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) similarly ties rescission to whether the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).” Read in context, that language makes the operative question for an in absentia order whether the noncitizen received a valid notice of the hearing that was actually missed—something a later § 1229(a)(2) notice can supply by providing the correct time and place. Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland construed § 1229(a)(1) in the stop-time and case-initiation context, but neither decision held that a defective initial NTA categorically bars in absentia removal notwithstanding later, proper hearing notice under § 1229(a)(2). A narrow ruling respecting the distinct statutory text Congress used for in absentia orders (and avoiding broader disruption to removal administration) supports affirmance where the later notice gave the time and place and the noncitizen failed to appear.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1229a(b)(5)(A) authorizes in absentia removal when the Government establishes that written notice was provided “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)” of § 1229(a), and § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) permits rescission only if the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).” Reading those provisions according to their ordinary meaning, a later notice of hearing that supplies the time and place information qualifies as notice “in accordance with” § 1229(a)(2), so an in absentia order may stand when the alien fails to appear after receiving that notice. Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland construed § 1229(a)(1)’s “notice to appear” requirement in the stop-time context and do not override Congress’s express disjunctive “(1) or (2)” framework for in absentia removal and rescission. Because Congress provided a separate mechanism in § 1229(a)(2) for time-and-place notice, the absence of that information in the initial NTA does not, by itself, compel rescission where proper § 1229(a)(2) notice was later given and ignored.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(b)(5)(A) authorizes an in absentia removal order when the noncitizen was provided written notice “under paragraph (1) or (2)” of § 1229(a), and § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) likewise ties rescission to whether the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).” That disjunctive structure makes clear that a later notice of hearing supplying the time and place under § 1229(a)(2) can suffice even if the initial NTA under § 1229(a)(1) lacked that information. Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland construed § 1229(a)(1) in the distinct stop-time context and did not rewrite the in absentia provisions to impose a single-document requirement where Congress instead expressly allowed notice via paragraph (1) or paragraph (2). As a practical matter consistent with the statute’s focus on attendance at the scheduled hearing, permitting rescission despite actual time-and-place notice would invalidate large numbers of orders based on paperwork defects unrelated to the missed hearing and would undermine orderly administration and enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1229(a)(1) defines a “Notice to Appear” as a single written notice specifying, among other things, the time and place of the hearing, and Niz-Chavez v. Garland held the government must provide that required information in one document rather than through a two-step notice process. Because § 1229a(b)(5) authorizes in absentia removal only when the noncitizen received “notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2),” a later hearing notice under § 1229(a)(2) cannot cure the government’s failure to provide a compliant § 1229(a)(1) Notice to Appear in the first place—especially where there has been no “change” of time or place to trigger paragraph (2). Allowing removal in absentia despite a defective initiating notice undermines fair process and predictably harms vulnerable noncitizens who may miss hearings or lose the ability to seek relief because the government did not follow Congress’s notice commands. Pereira and Niz-Chavez confirm that Congress insisted on clear, time-and-place-specific notice, and the remedy for noncompliance in this context is rescission of an in absentia order for lack of proper notice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(A) authorizes in absentia removal when the noncitizen was provided written notice of the proceeding “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)” of § 1229(a), and § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) correspondingly allows rescission only upon a showing the person did not receive notice “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).” Read in that context, a later notice of hearing that supplies the time and place and warns of the consequences of nonappearance fits § 1229(a)(2)’s content requirements and can provide the notice necessary to support an in absentia order for the hearing that was missed, even if the initial NTA was deficient under § 1229(a)(1). Pereira and Niz-Chavez interpreted “notice to appear” in § 1229(a)(1) for the stop-time rule and held that a deficient NTA cannot be cured by later papers for that purpose; they do not compel importing a single-document requirement into § 1229a(b)(5), which expressly contemplates notice under either paragraph (1) or paragraph (2). This reading better matches the statute’s workability and coherence by tying in absentia consequences to whether the person received notice of the specific hearing at which removal was ordered.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The controlling text for in absentia removal and rescission is 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(b)(5), which authorizes an in absentia order when the Government establishes by clear, unequivocal, and convincing evidence that the noncitizen received the “written notice required under paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a)” for the hearing that was missed. Whatever defects existed in the initial § 1229(a)(1) Notice to Appear, a later notice of hearing supplying the correct time and place fits § 1229(a)(2)’s notice mechanism and thus satisfies the “(1) or (2)” condition Congress expressly wrote into § 1229a(b)(5). Pereira and Niz-Chavez held that a deficient NTA cannot trigger the stop-time rule under § 1229b(d)(1) because that provision turns on service of “a” notice to appear under § 1229(a)(1), but that reasoning does not override § 1229a(b)(5)’s different, disjunctive notice trigger that expressly includes paragraph (2). Reading § 1229a(b)(5) as allowing in absentia removal where a valid § 1229(a)(2) notice provided the time and place for the missed hearing follows the statute’s plain meaning and avoids importing stop-time-rule-specific logic into a differently worded provision.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5) expressly authorizes an in absentia removal order when the Government shows that “written notice required under paragraph (1) or paragraph (2)” was provided, and likewise ties rescission to whether the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).” Read in context, that language focuses the in absentia inquiry on whether the noncitizen received the operative hearing notice—time and place—through either a compliant § 1229(a)(1) NTA or a later § 1229(a)(2) notice, rather than treating an earlier NTA defect as categorically fatal. Pereira and Niz-Chavez construed what makes an NTA sufficient for the stop-time rule and emphasized a “single-document” requirement for § 1229(a)(1), but they did not address § 1229a(b)(5)’s distinct, disjunctive “(1) or (2)” notice scheme or require rescission where the noncitizen in fact received a later, correct hearing notice and then failed to appear. Given workability and Congress’s explicit allowance of paragraph (2) notice in the in absentia provisions, I would uphold the removal order and deny rescission when proper § 1229(a)(2) notice was later sent and not heeded.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(A) authorizes in absentia removal when the Government provides written notice “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” and § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) likewise ties rescission to whether the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).” Reading that text as written, receipt of a later notice specifying the hearing’s time and place under § 1229(a)(2) can satisfy the notice predicate for an in absentia order and foreclose rescission, even if the initial NTA was defective under § 1229(a)(1). Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland construed § 1229(a)(1) in the distinct stop-time/case-initiating context and do not justify rewriting the in absentia provisions’ express disjunctive (“or (2)”) to require a single, compliant NTA for all purposes. The statutory structure—paragraph (2) supplying operative time-and-place information for the hearing actually missed—supports the Attorney General’s position that the relevant inquiry is whether the noncitizen received the hearing notice required by § 1229(a)(1) or § 1229(a)(2).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(A) authorizes in absentia removal when the government establishes that written notice was provided “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)” of § 1229(a), and § 1229(a)(2) specifically contemplates a later written notice supplying the “new time or place of the proceedings.” While Pereira and Niz-Chavez require a single, time-and-place-complete Notice to Appear for the stop-time rule, those cases construed a different statutory mechanism and do not clearly negate Congress’s express “(1) or (2)” notice framework for in absentia orders and rescission under § 1229a(b)(5). On a pragmatic and procedural-fairness view, if the noncitizen actually received the later notice of hearing specifying the time and place and still failed to appear, rescission would not serve the statute’s core due-process function of ensuring meaningful notice, and would impose substantial administrative costs without a corresponding fairness gain. I would therefore uphold in absentia removal (and deny rescission) where the government proves proper service of the later § 1229(a)(2) hearing notice for the missed hearing, notwithstanding defects in the initial NTA under § 1229(a)(1).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a noncitizen can rescind an in absentia removal order for lack of notice when the government did not provide a single notice containing the hearing’s time-and-place information in the initial “notice to appear,” but the noncitizen later received a separate notice of hearing with the correct time and place and still failed to appear.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. §§ 1229(a)(1)–(2) (notice requirements) and 1229a(b)(5) (in absentia removal; rescission for lack of notice).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Campos-Chaves (and similarly situated noncitizens in the consolidated cases) argues that the statutory “notice” required to sustain or bar rescission of an in absentia removal order must comply with 8 U.S.C. § 1229(a)(1) in the first instance—i.e., a valid Notice to Appear must include the time and place of the hearing. If the initial NTA omitted that information, then—even if a later notice of hearing provided time and place—the noncitizen should still be able to rescind an in absentia order on the ground that he did not receive the statutorily required notice.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that under 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(b)(5), a noncitizen who actually received notice of the time and place of the specific hearing he missed (via a later notice under § 1229(a)(2)) cannot rescind an in absentia removal order by pointing to a defect in the earlier NTA; the “lack of notice” rescission remedy focuses on whether the noncitizen received notice of the hearing at which he failed to appear, not on whether the initial charging document was perfectly compliant with § 1229(a)(1). The government also argues that statutory context, practicality/common sense, and (if ambiguity remains) deference principles favor its reading.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest contention is that Pereira and Niz-Chavez require treating a time-and-place–omitting NTA as not “in accordance with” § 1229(a)(1) and forbid any later “cure,” lest paragraph (1)’s requirements become optional. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) is written disjunctively—rescission turns on whether the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2),” and paragraph (2) is expressly designed to provide the time-and-place notice for the particular hearing that results in an in absentia order. Pereira and Niz-Chavez construed the stop-time rule’s reference to “a notice to appear,” and extending their single-document rule into this distinct, hearing-specific rescission framework would be an unnecessary expansion that risks reading “or (2)” out of the statute and upsetting settled in absentia administration despite actual notice of the missed hearing. A narrow holding—limited to cases where the alien received a compliant § 1229(a)(2) notice of the hearing missed—best preserves precedent without importing it beyond its context and protects institutional legitimacy by deciding no more than necessary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Pereira and Niz-Chavez insist Congress meant what it said when defining a “notice to appear” in § 1229(a)(1), and she warns that allowing later notices makes proper commencement “optional.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) uses an expressly disjunctive rescission trigger—nonreceipt of notice “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)”—and an original public-meaning reading cannot treat “or (2)” as surplusage by making any initial § 1229(a)(1) defect dispositive even where a compliant § 1229(a)(2) hearing notice was received. Pereira/Niz-Chavez interpreted a different cross-reference (“a notice to appear under § 1229(a)”) in the stop-time rule and do not justify rewriting this separate, hearing-specific rescission standard into a freestanding sanction for defective charging paperwork. Paragraph (2) is not textually limited to “changes after proper commencement,” and importing that limitation would add words Congress did not enact, contrary to textualism.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Pereira and Niz-Chavez insist an NTA missing time and place is not “in accordance with” § 1229(a)(1), and she worries allowing later notices makes paragraph (1)’s requirements optional. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) is expressly disjunctive—rescission turns on whether the noncitizen did not receive notice under paragraph (1) or paragraph (2)—so receipt of a proper § 1229(a)(2) hearing notice defeats the “lack of notice” ground even if the initial NTA was defective. Pereira/Niz-Chavez arose in the stop-time context and do not justify importing a one-document rule that would effectively nullify Congress’s separate authorization for hearing-specific notice via paragraph (2) in the in absentia scheme. Extending Sotomayor’s reading would convert a targeted notice remedy into a broad sanction for earlier paperwork defects despite actual notice of the hearing missed, a disruptive result Congress did not clearly command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) uses a disjunctive “(1) or (2)” and that paragraph (2) can supply time-and-place notice for a particular hearing, but their reading still leaves “in accordance with paragraph (1)” doing almost no work where proceedings were never properly commenced by a compliant § 1229(a)(1) notice to appear. Pereira and Niz-Chavez matter here not because they mechanically export a “single-document” rule, but because they insist we respect Congress’s definition of an NTA in § 1229(a)(1) when Congress incorporates that term—otherwise the government can obtain in absentia orders without ever providing the initiating notice Congress specified, a practical burden that falls hardest on unrepresented and vulnerable respondents. Justice Gorsuch’s surplusage concern can be met by treating paragraph (2) as independently sufficient only when it functions as Congress designed—i.e., as notice of changes/postponements after valid initiation—not as a workaround that retroactively sanitizes a defective commencement. Given the stakes of in absentia removal and the statute’s notice-protective architecture, I do not think actual receipt of a later (a)(2) notice should categorically defeat rescission when the government never served a valid (a)(1) NTA to start with.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Pereira and Niz-Chavez insist we take § 1229(a)(1)’s time-and-place requirements seriously and not treat them as optional. But those cases construed a different cross-reference (“a notice to appear” in the stop-time rule), whereas § 1229a(b)(5)(A) and (C)(ii) repeatedly and expressly hinge in absentia consequences and rescission on whether notice was provided under paragraph (1) or paragraph (2), making the inquiry hearing-specific and giving independent work to “or (2),” as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize. Sotomayor’s attempt to cabin paragraph (2) to “changes/postponements after proper commencement” isn’t anchored in the text of (C)(ii), which does not condition paragraph (2)’s sufficiency on a valid paragraph (1) NTA. On a pragmatic textualist reading, rescission for “lack of notice” should track whether the person received compliant notice of the hearing he missed, and where a proper § 1229(a)(2) notice was received, reopening becomes an untethered sanction for earlier paperwork defects rather than a cure for notice failure.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Pereira and Niz-Chavez took seriously Congress’s definition of a notice to appear in § 1229(a)(1) and rejected after-the-fact "curing" in that stop-time context. But here, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) asks a different, hearing-specific question—whether the noncitizen "did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)"—and giving operative effect to the disjunctive "or (2)" means receipt of a compliant § 1229(a)(2) hearing notice defeats rescission even if the initial NTA was defective. Sotomayor’s effort to confine paragraph (2) to changes after proper commencement adds atextual limitations; paragraph (2) by its terms governs notice of the "time and place" of "the proceedings" and thus directly addresses the notice needed for the particular hearing missed. On a textualist and originalist reading attentive to context and avoiding surplusage, importing Niz-Chavez’s single-document rule into this separate rescission provision would transform a narrow lack-of-notice remedy into a broad sanction untethered to actual notice of the hearing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Pereira and Niz-Chavez took Congress’s time-and-place requirement in § 1229(a)(1) seriously and rejected a general "cure" theory in the stop-time context, and her point about protecting unrepresented noncitizens carries real equitable force. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(A) and (C)(ii) are written disjunctively—notice "in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)"—and in this in absentia/rescission framework Congress made receipt of hearing-specific notice (which § 1229(a)(2) supplies) independently sufficient. Under my institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, Pereira/Niz-Chavez should be kept cabined to the stop-time rule’s distinct cross-reference to "a notice to appear under § 1229(a)" and not extended to override the separate structure Congress enacted for in absentia orders. Reading (C)(ii) to mandate rescission despite undisputed receipt of a proper § 1229(a)(2) hearing notice would effectively erase "or (2)" and invite significant administrative disruption without a clear statutory command.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness and Pereira/Niz-Chavez-based argument is the most serious challenge, but those precedents construed the stop-time rule’s reference to “a notice to appear under § 1229(a)” and do not supply a textual basis to rewrite § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), which expressly turns on whether the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the in absentia and rescission provisions are structured hearing-specifically, and paragraph (2) is not surplus: it is Congress’s mechanism for time-and-place notice for the hearing at issue, including where the initial NTA lacked that information. Justice Sotomayor’s reading would effectively treat any paragraph (1) defect as dispositive even when paragraph (2) notice was actually received, draining the disjunctive “or (2)” of operative meaning and converting a “lack of notice” remedy into a sanction untethered to the missed hearing. Under an original public meaning and anti-surplusage approach, the better reading is that receipt of a compliant § 1229(a)(2) notice defeats rescission under § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-based warning—that letting a later notice “cure” a defective NTA effectively makes § 1229(a)(1)’s requirements optional and disproportionately harms unrepresented people—has real force, and Pereira/Niz-Chavez underscore Congress’s insistence on clarity. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) is written to make rescission turn on whether the person “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2),” which pragmatically focuses on notice of the specific hearing missed—exactly what § 1229(a)(2) supplies. On my procedural-fairness, consequences-sensitive approach, reopening in absentia orders despite actual receipt of accurate time-and-place hearing notice would convert a “lack of notice” remedy into a sanction for charging-document defects, untethered to the reliability of the absence determination. Pereira/Niz-Chavez therefore inform the importance of administrable notice rules, but they do not overcome the distinct, disjunctive structure Congress chose for in absentia rescission.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) allows rescission for “lack of notice” of the hearing at which the noncitizen failed to appear, and § 1229a(b)(5)(A) similarly authorizes an in absentia order when written notice was provided under § 1229(a)(1) or § 1229(a)(2), indicating Congress focused on actual notice of the missed hearing rather than technical defects in the initial charging document. Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland construed § 1229(a)(1)’s “notice to appear” requirement in the distinct stop-time context (§ 1229b(d)(1)) and do not compel treating a later, accurate § 1229(a)(2) notice of hearing as irrelevant for in absentia rescission. A narrow ruling preserving the in absentia framework while respecting the statutory disjunctive “or” avoids expanding Pereira/Niz-Chavez beyond their context and better serves institutional legitimacy and administrability. Where the noncitizen received a proper notice of hearing with the correct time and place and still did not appear, the statutory “lack of notice” remedy does not apply.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The rescission provision turns on whether the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), and paragraph (2) expressly governs later notice supplying the “time and place” of proceedings. Where, as here, the noncitizen actually received a § 1229(a)(2) notice of hearing with the correct time-and-place for the hearing he missed, he cannot plausibly claim “lack of notice” as to that hearing, even if the initial charging document was defective under § 1229(a)(1). Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland addressed what qualifies as a “notice to appear” for the stop-time rule and do not rewrite § 1229a(b)(5) to make rescission hinge on a single-document requirement when the relevant hearing notice was in fact provided. Textually, tying rescission to a prior paperwork defect would expand the statutory remedy beyond its limited function—correcting removals entered without notice of the missed hearing—and would improperly elevate form over the notice Congress required.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) authorizes rescission only upon a showing that the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” and that disjunctive text focuses on whether he received notice of the hearing he missed, not on whether the initial charging document complied in a single instrument with § 1229(a)(1). When the government later serves a § 1229(a)(2) notice of hearing providing the correct time and place, and the noncitizen nonetheless fails to appear, the practical and law-enforcement consequences of allowing rescission based solely on an earlier defect would be substantial and inconsistent with Congress’s in absentia scheme in § 1229a(b)(5). Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland construed § 1229(a)(1)’s requirements in the distinct context of the stop-time rule and the meaning of a “notice to appear,” but they do not compel importing a one-document rule into § 1229a(b)(5)’s separate “(1) or (2)” rescission standard. Reading the statute as a whole, an alien who actually received the time-and-place notice for the missed hearing cannot claim “lack of notice” under § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) merely because the earlier NTA omitted that information.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) allows rescission of an in absentia removal order when the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” and § 1229(a)(1) defines the required “notice to appear” to include the time-and-place information. Under Niz-Chavez v. Garland and Pereira v. Sessions, a document labeled an NTA that omits time and place is not the statutorily required notice to appear and cannot be “cured” for that statutory function by a later, separate document; Congress chose a clear, administrable notice rule that protects fairness and access to court. Reading the “lack of notice” rescission remedy to tolerate an invalid initiating notice would dilute Congress’s command and disproportionately burden vulnerable, often unrepresented noncitizens navigating complex proceedings. The government has ample remedial tools—serve a compliant single-document NTA—to avoid this problem, and the statutory text as construed in Niz-Chavez counsels in favor of permitting rescission here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) permits rescission only when the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” and the disjunctive “or” most naturally focuses the inquiry on whether the person received notice of the specific hearing he missed—here supplied by a later § 1229(a)(2) notice of hearing with the correct time and place. Pereira and Niz-Chavez construed § 1229(a)(1) for the stop-time rule and required a single compliant “notice to appear” there, but they did not hold that a defect in the initial charging document nullifies otherwise proper notice of the hearing for in absentia purposes under § 1229a(b)(5). Reading the rescission remedy to turn on actual receipt of time-and-place notice promotes statutory coherence with § 1229a(b)(5)(A)’s in absentia authorization and yields a more workable rule than reopening cases where the noncitizen had timely, correct hearing notice yet failed to appear. Given the statute’s structure and the practical function of § 1229(a)(2) notices, I would not extend Niz-Chavez’s “single document” requirement to override § 1229a(b)(5)’s notice-focused rescission scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) authorizes rescission only when the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” which naturally focuses on whether he received the notice specifying the “time and place” of the particular hearing he missed; here, that information was supplied in a later notice under § 1229(a)(2). Pereira and Niz-Chavez construed what counts as “a notice to appear” under § 1229(a)(1) (including the single-document requirement), but they did not rewrite § 1229a(b)(5) to make an initial paperwork defect categorically negate later, hearing-specific notice that Congress separately authorized in § 1229(a)(2). Reading “or (2)” to have independent operative effect respects the statute’s plain text and avoids converting a remedial “lack of notice” provision into a free-standing sanction for defective charging documents. Where the noncitizen actually received time-and-place notice of the hearing and still failed to appear, the rule of lenity has no work to do because the text is best read to foreclose rescission.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5) authorizes in absentia removal when the noncitizen is provided written notice “in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)” of § 1229(a), and the rescission remedy for “lack of notice” likewise turns on whether the noncitizen received notice of the specific hearing he missed—not whether the initial charging NTA was a single, perfectly compliant document under § 1229(a)(1). Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland applied a “single document” rule in the distinct stop-time context of § 1229b(d)(1), and they did not purport to rewrite § 1229a(b)(5)’s disjunctive structure permitting notice via § 1229(a)(2). Given precedent’s limited reach, the statutory text’s focus on actual hearing notice, and the practical workability/legitimacy concerns of vacating in absentia orders despite undisputed receipt of a timely notice of hearing, I would affirm the government’s position. Judicial restraint counsels against extending Pereira/Niz-Chavez beyond their context to create a broad rescission remedy Congress did not clearly provide in § 1229a(b)(5).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) allows rescission only if the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” and paragraph (2) specifically governs notice of the “time and place” of the hearing at issue, so receipt of a proper § 1229(a)(2) notice of hearing defeats a claimed “lack of notice” for the missed hearing. Read in context, § 1229a(b)(5) focuses on whether the noncitizen received notice of “the time and place of the proceedings” at which he failed to appear, not whether the initial charging NTA perfectly complied with § 1229(a)(1). Pereira and Niz-Chavez construed “notice to appear under § 1229(a)” in the distinct stop-time setting and do not compel importing a single-document rule into § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) where Congress expressly allowed notice via paragraph (1) “or (2).” Giving effect to the disjunctive “or” and the remedial purpose of the rescission provision, a noncitizen who actually received time-and-place notice for the hearing cannot rescind solely due to an earlier NTA defect.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) authorizes rescission of an in absentia removal order only upon a showing that the noncitizen “did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of section 1229(a),” which pragmatically focuses on whether the person received notice of the specific hearing at which he failed to appear. Even if the initial Notice to Appear was defective under § 1229(a)(1), receipt of a later Notice of Hearing providing the correct time and place under § 1229(a)(2) generally satisfies the statute’s core procedural-fairness function for the missed hearing, making rescission an ill-fitting remedy where actual notice was provided and ignored. Pereira v. Sessions and Niz-Chavez v. Garland construed “a notice to appear under § 1229(a)” in the stop-time context to require a single document, but they did not resolve the distinct in absentia rescission scheme that expressly contemplates notice under either § 1229(a)(1) or § 1229(a)(2). Considering practical consequences for orderly adjudication and the statute’s hearing-specific notice focus, I would not extend the single-document rule to mandate rescission where the noncitizen received the correct hearing notice and still failed to appear.
